strengths: The post-hoc repair formulation is practical: LPAM can augment existing stitching pipelines without retraining or modifying their alignment models.
The pipeline is coherent and clearly illustrated, combining seam-quality detection, localized SIFT-flow refinement, tapered warping, and boundary-constrained local seam merging.
Experiments cover 79 pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods. All reported within-system comparisons improve across RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC.
The paper includes parameter ablations, CPU runtime measurements, qualitative failure analysis, appropriate citations for reused components, and a public code link.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is not independent of the method: metrics compare the two locally warped source patches along the selected seam, while LPAM explicitly warps those patches to increase their agreement and uses SSIM for detection. Better scores therefore do not necessarily imply a less distorted or more perceptually convincing final mosaic.

Final-output quality is inadequately validated. There is no ground truth, user study, or independent perceptual evaluation, no uncertainty or significance analysis, and only one main-paper qualitative comparison against Parallax and SEAGULL. This is insufficient for the broad superiority and robustness claims.

Originality is moderate. The method largely composes SSIM, Otsu thresholding, SIFT flow, sigmoid tapering, and graph cuts, while seam-guided local alignment is already represented by SEAGULL. The useful distinction is modular post-processing, but claims of a new paradigm, complete dissociation from initial alignment, and compatibility with arbitrary seam-cutting pipelines are overstated.

The detection rule can label a uniformly high-error seam as plausible whenever its maximum is near its mean. The fixed factor k=1.5 and Otsu-based selection are not ablated, and the assertion that false positives cannot worsen results is unsupported.

Important technical details are unclear or problematic: the exact patch-expansion rule and SIFT-flow settings are omitted; Eq. (3)'s exact photometric equality is not guaranteed by SIFT flow; the sigmoid has nonzero/nonunit finite endpoints; and only horizontal coordinate tapering is described. The authors also show that small extracted patches can fail.

The ablation exposes an evaluation mismatch: removing the sigmoid often gives better seam-agreement metrics but creates visible boundary artifacts. Choosing β=8 from limited qualitative evidence leaves the key alignment-versus-distortion tradeoff unresolved.

The runtime table appears to report LPAM time separately rather than total pipeline time, despite '+LPAM' labeling. Input resolutions are unspecified, and adding 6–10 seconds roughly doubles several host methods, weakening the efficiency claim.
The authors' 20-pair dataset lacks acquisition, selection, licensing, and release details in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility and assessment of dataset bias.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical weakness of seam-cutting pipelines and proposes a coherent modular remedy: SSIM-based failure detection, localized SIFT-flow alignment, boundary-attenuated warping, and constrained local seam merging.

The evaluation has useful breadth: 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five initial alignment methods. Tables 1 and 2 report consistent improvements across all tested combinations.
The parameter ablations, CPU timing, explicit failure example, and public code link are valuable for understanding robustness and reproducibility.
The presentation is generally clear, with effective pipeline diagrams and appropriate attribution of the main alignment, correspondence, and graph-cut components.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative metrics are measured along the adaptively selected seam after LPAM has warped the underlying patches—the same local agreement the method directly optimizes. They do not establish perceptual quality, content preservation, or geometric plausibility of the final mosaic. No user study, output-level evaluation, uncertainty estimates, or per-image statistics are provided.

End-to-end comparison against Parallax and SEAGULL is limited to one selected visual example, while recent methods cited as references [5] and [35] are not experimentally compared. Consequently, the broad claims of superiority and dissociation from initial alignment accuracy are insufficiently supported.

The technical novelty is modest because LPAM mainly combines established SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT flow, and graph-cut seam estimation. The claimed applicability to arbitrary seam-cutting pipelines is demonstrated empirically for several methods but not justified generally.

Several important details or edge cases are unresolved. A uniformly poor seam can satisfy max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) and be incorrectly accepted; the sigmoid construction is defined only for horizontal alignment; Eq. (3)'s exact photometric equality is unrealistic; and patch padding, overlapping-component order, interpolation, SIFT-flow settings, and guarantees of seam connectivity are not specified adequately.

The ablation exposes a metric mismatch: removing sigmoid attenuation gives the best numerical scores, while beta=8 is selected from a qualitative artifact example without systematic boundary-artifact evaluation. The fixed detection constant k is not ablated.

The runtime table appears to report LPAM time separately rather than total integrated runtime, despite the '+LPAM' notation. Image resolutions, memory use, and full pipeline costs are omitted, making the computational-efficiency claim difficult to assess. Details and provenance for the new 20-pair dataset are also limited.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant practical failure mode: a globally reasonable warp can remain locally misaligned where a stitching seam passes. Refining only those neighborhoods is intuitive and potentially useful.

LPAM is modular and is evaluated with four seam-cutting methods, five alignment methods, and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. Tables 1 and 2 show consistent improvements in the authors' seam-local metrics.

The pipeline is reasonably clear and uses well-attributed components: SSIM-based detection, Otsu thresholding, SIFT Flow, and constrained graph-cut seam recomputation. An algorithm, parameter studies, runtime measurements, and a code link are provided.
The authors disclose an important failure mode involving the tradeoff between accurate local alignment and continuity at patch boundaries.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evaluation is not independent of the method. LPAM explicitly warps patches to increase correspondence near the seam, and performance is then measured using RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC on those same locally modified seam neighborhoods. These metrics neither assess distortion introduced within the selected source region nor artifacts at patch boundaries or elsewhere in the final mosaic.

Table 3 exposes this evaluation mismatch: removing the sigmoid boundary-smoothing mechanism gives substantially better reported metrics on every dataset, yet the authors select beta=8 based on a qualitative artifact example. Without a human study, ground-truth evaluation, or credible full-output perceptual metric, the central claim of improved final stitching quality remains insufficiently supported.

Comparison with complete competing systems is weak. Parallax and SEAGULL are shown on only one detailed qualitative example, with no dataset-level quantitative or user-study comparison. Tables 1 and 2 mainly compare each pipeline against itself after adding LPAM, so they do not establish the claimed superiority over state of the art.

The technical novelty is modest relative to prior seam-guided local alignment and dense-flow seam methods. The method combines established tools in a useful way, but claims of a new paradigm, independence from initial alignment, and applicability to arbitrary seam-cutting pipelines are overstated.

Several heuristics limit robustness. The max-to-mean test declares a uniformly high-error seam acceptable; SSIM can confuse exposure changes with geometric error; SIFT Flow has no stated occlusion or confidence handling; and the fixed coordinate-wise sigmoid construction is described only for horizontal patches. The method still assumes that initial alignment is sufficiently good and fails under larger local displacement, as Figure 6 acknowledges.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence are incomplete: patch-enclosure rules, overlap/update handling, flow and graph-cut settings, and the treatment of other patch orientations are underspecified; the new dataset is only briefly depicted; and results lack per-image distributions, uncertainty, or significance tests. Runtime reporting also gives LPAM and host-method times separately rather than clearly reporting end-to-end integrated cost.

The evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five upstream alignment methods. Tables 1–2 report directionally consistent average improvements in all four seam-similarity metrics.
LPAM is modular and interpretable, and the paper includes parameter ablations, CPU timings, a failure example, a limitations discussion, and a public code link.
The presentation is generally concise and visually clear, with appropriate citations for the principal datasets and reused components such as SSIM, SIFT Flow, and graph cuts.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is not a convincing measure of final stitching quality. RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC are evaluated between patches from the two locally rewarped images along the selected seam; SSIM also drives patch selection, while SIFT Flow is explicitly introduced to increase local correspondence. Better scores are therefore largely expected and do not establish that the final mosaic is perceptually better or geometrically faithful. No ground-truth evaluation, user study, or independent perceptual/artifact assessment is provided.

Comparative evidence is inadequate for the claimed superiority. Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a single qualitative comparison in Fig. 7, with no quantitative full-output comparison. Results are reported only as dataset means, without variances, confidence intervals, per-image outcomes, or counts of cases that deteriorate. This cannot support the claimed robustness across challenging cases.

The seam-failure detector is technically fragile. A seam with uniformly large error can satisfy max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) and be declared plausible because the test is relative rather than absolute. Conversely, SSIM can respond to exposure changes or occlusions that alignment cannot resolve. Neither the detector, k=1.5, nor the Otsu decision is validated or ablated.

The sigmoid construction does not justify the claimed smooth insertion of a two-dimensional patch. It tapers flow only along the horizontal coordinate, leaving possible discontinuities at the top and bottom boundaries; its endpoint values are not exactly zero and one either. Figure 6 confirms that boundary artifacts occur. Equation (3)'s asserted exact photometric equality is also invalid under illumination changes, occlusion, or imperfect correspondence.

The originality is limited and insufficiently established. LPAM combines established SSIM/Otsu thresholding, SIFT Flow, a sigmoid taper, and graph-cut seam selection. Closely related seam-guided local alignment and dense-flow seam estimation are acknowledged, but no controlled comparison demonstrates a substantive distinction. The claims of being the first framework and supporting arbitrary seam-cutting are especially unsupported; experiments cover a narrow family of two-image graph-cut pipelines.

Important implementation details are absent: how component-enclosing patches and margins are chosen, treatment of overlapping patches and processing order, vertical or differently oriented overlaps, SIFT-Flow parameters and confidence/occlusion handling, interpolation and image-boundary rules, the local seam energy, and exact SSIM/color conventions. The custom dataset lacks a collection protocol, release statement, and licensing information. A code link helps but does not make the manuscript itself reproducible.

The ablation and efficiency evidence undercut the selected design and claims. Removing the sigmoid is better in 10 of the 12 reported metric/dataset combinations, yet the choice of beta=8 is justified using only one qualitative example. Table 4 reports host seam-cutting and LPAM times separately under confusing '+LPAM' labels; integrated runtime is not reported. Adding roughly 6–10 seconds would double or triple several host runtimes, so the characterization as lightweight or computationally efficient is not adequately supported.

The claim that LPAM 'dissociates' seam quality from initial alignment accuracy is overstated: it still requires sufficient local overlap and reliable dense correspondence, and the admitted failure case demonstrates sensitivity to the initial geometry and patch extent. strengths: The paper targets a practical failure mode: conventional seam cutting cannot recover when the initial warp is locally inaccurate. A modular post-alignment correction could be useful for existing stitching systems.

LPAM is conceptually simple and understandable, combining seam-quality screening, localized SIFT-flow alignment, tapered deformation, and boundary-constrained local seam cutting. The figures and algorithm communicate the overall pipeline reasonably well.

The evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five initial alignment methods. Tables 1 and 2 show consistent improvements in all reported seam-agreement metrics.
The authors provide parameter ablations, CPU timing, a failure example, an explicit limitation, citations to the principal components, and a code link, all of which are helpful for verification.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is not sufficiently independent. LPAM directly warps patches to increase local correspondence, after which RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC are measured between those modified patches along the newly selected seam; SSIM also drives patch selection. These results demonstrate increased local agreement but do not establish that the final mosaic is perceptually better or geometrically faithful. A degenerate method that copies or strongly deforms content near the seam could score well. Ground-truth evaluation, a perceptual study, or an independent final-image criterion is needed.

Dataset-level comparisons against complete state-of-the-art pipelines are absent. Parallax and SEAGULL are compared visually on only one example in Figure 7, while Tables 1 and 2 report only before/after LPAM variants. Consequently, claims of superiority and comparability to seam-driven methods are not convincingly supported or protected against qualitative example selection.

Originality appears modest relative to ICCV standards: SSIM thresholding, SIFT Flow, sigmoid deformation tapering, and graph-cut seam estimation are established tools. The distinction from the closely related seam-guided local alignment of SEAGULL and the dense-matching seam method in reference 35 is insufficiently analyzed. Claims of a novel paradigm that 'dissociates' seam quality from alignment accuracy are overstated because LPAM still depends on successful dense local alignment.

Several technical details are underspecified or questionable. The manuscript does not precisely define patch margins and orientation, vertical cases, SIFT-flow parameters/objective, interpolation and occlusion handling, local pairwise seam costs, or treatment of overlapping components. Equation 3 assumes exact RGB correspondence, which is generally false and is not the SIFT-flow objective. The one-dimensional sigmoid does not exactly reach zero or one and offers no explicit continuity guarantee at the other patch boundaries.

The SSIM/Otsu detector is heuristic and unvalidated. SSIM can respond to exposure changes, occlusions, or genuine scene differences rather than geometric error; the fixed k=1.5 threshold has no sensitivity study or detection-quality evaluation. The assertion that false positives cannot yield inferior results conflicts with the acknowledged possibility of newly introduced boundary artifacts.

The ablation does not fully justify the selected configuration. Removing the sigmoid gives substantially better reported metrics, and beta=16 often matches or exceeds beta=8; the preference for beta=8 rests mainly on limited qualitative evidence. There are no ablations of the detector, Otsu threshold, dense matcher, or constrained seam-merging components.

Reporting is insufficient for robustness and efficiency claims: only aggregate means are given without variance, significance, or per-image win rates; the new 20-pair dataset lacks acquisition, release, and provenance details. (5) does not attain 0 and 1 at the patch boundaries as the accompanying text suggests.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical failure mode of seam-cutting pipelines and proposes an intuitive localized remedy: detect problematic seam segments, refine their alignment with dense flow, and reconnect the seam using boundary-constrained graph cuts.

The modular design is potentially useful. LPAM is tested with four seam-cutting methods, five initial alignment methods, and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs, with consistent improvements in all reported seam-similarity metrics.
The manuscript includes parameter ablations, CPU timing, qualitative examples, and an informative failure case. A public code link further supports reproducibility.
The presentation is generally clear, with an effective overview figure and algorithmic summary, and the relevant datasets and component methods are mostly attributed appropriately.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence does not convincingly establish perceptual stitching quality. RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC are computed between the two locally warped images around the final seam—the exact region LPAM explicitly aligns—so improvement is partly built into the evaluation. Table 3 exposes this problem: removing the sigmoid taper produces substantially better seam metrics while introducing visible boundary artifacts. Full-mosaic perceptual evaluation or a controlled user study is needed.

The qualitative evidence in the main paper is limited, with only one comprehensive full-result comparison, and there are no per-image results, confidence intervals, statistical tests, user preferences, or aggregate failure rates. Thus, it is unclear how consistently the numerical gains translate into better mosaics.

Originality is modest: the method combines SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT Flow, sigmoid-tapered warping, and graph-cut seam estimation. The claimed first modular framework and alignment-independent paradigm are not convincingly distinguished from closely related seam-guided local alignment and dense-matching approaches such as references [22], [35], and the highly relevant [5]. Recent alternatives also receive no quantitative comparison.

The failure detector uses only relative variation along a seam: a uniformly severe error can satisfy max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) and be declared plausible. Its assumption that failures are always localized is not validated, and robustness to exposure changes, occlusions, repeated textures, or incorrect dense flow is not evaluated.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including correction-patch dimensions and padding, handling of vertical or arbitrarily oriented regions, overlapping components, interpolation and out-of-bounds flow, and the smoothness energy used for local seam cutting. Equation (3) also inaccurately describes SIFT Flow as producing exact RGB equality, weakening the technical exposition and manuscript-level reproducibility.

The ablation mostly sweeps hyperparameters rather than isolating the detector, dense alignment, tapering, and local re-cutting contributions. The selected beta is not consistently optimal in Table 3, and parameter selection appears to use the same datasets on which final performance is reported.

The efficiency claim is overstated. Table 4 reports LPAM time separately rather than end-to-end combined runtime; its additional 6–10 seconds approximately doubles several inexpensive seam cutters. Image resolutions and runtime variability are omitted. The authors' 20-pair dataset is also insufficiently documented with respect to capture protocol, availability, and licensing.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine image-stitching failure mode: a globally reasonable warp can remain locally misaligned where a seam must pass. LPAM is a practical, training-free post-processing module that can be attached to several seam-cutting pipelines.

The evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five initial alignment methods. Tables 1 and 2 report consistently favorable changes across all tested combinations rather than only one favorable baseline.
The pipeline is intuitive and generally well illustrated. The manuscript also provides parameter ablations, CPU runtimes, a failure case, a limitations discussion, and a public code link.
weaknesses: The originality is limited relative to the claims. LPAM combines established SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT Flow, sigmoid-weighted warping, and constrained graph-cut seam estimation. Closely related seam-guided local alignment and dense-matching seam methods are cited, especially [22] and [35], but the distinction is not developed convincingly and [35] receives no direct comparison. Claims of a new paradigm, the first modular framework, and dissociation from initial alignment are overstated because LPAM still depends critically on the initial warp, seam, and local correspondence quality.

The principal evaluation is substantially confounded. RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC are computed between the two locally modified images around each method's selected seam—the very discrepancy LPAM is designed to reduce. The before/after measurements can also use different seams and pixels. These metrics therefore do not assess geometric distortion, discontinuities around patch boundaries, duplicated content, or perceptual quality of the final mosaic. No user study, ground-truth evaluation, or independent perceptual assessment is provided. Table 3 reinforces this concern: removing the sigmoid gives substantially better values on most metrics, yet the authors reject that variant based on artifacts the metrics fail to capture.

The quality trigger has a clear failure mode: a seam is declared plausible when max(Q) is at most 1.5 times mean(Q). A uniformly high-error seam can satisfy this relative test and receive no correction. Thus the procedure detects localized outliers rather than generally detecting a poor seam, contrary to the broad large-parallax claims.

Several technical claims or specifications are inadequate. Equation 3 presents an exact intensity equality that is not the SIFT Flow objective; the sigmoid does not reach zero or one at patch boundaries and varies only horizontally, so it does not guarantee boundary continuity as claimed. Patch margins, orientation, overlapping-patch order, image-boundary handling, the actual graph-cut penalties, and SIFT Flow settings are not specified. The assertion that false-positive realignment cannot degrade results is unsupported and implausible under occlusion, repeated texture, or moving objects.

The experiments report only dataset means, without dispersion, statistical tests, or failure rates. The detailed full-mosaic comparison is essentially one selected example, and there is no quantitative full-system comparison with the closest recent methods. The 20-pair proprietary dataset lacks a collection protocol, resolution statistics, release statement, and licensing information. Dynamic scenes, illumination changes, and severe or spatially extensive misalignment are not systematically evaluated.

The efficiency evidence is ambiguously presented: Table 4's '+LPAM' rows appear to be module-only rather than total pipeline runtimes. A 6–10 second module can double or triple the cost of several listed seam cutters, while initial alignment is excluded, making the efficiency claim insufficiently supported. Overall, the method is promising as an engineering heuristic, but the limited novelty and non-independent evidence leave a slight preference for rejection.

weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is not an independent measure of final stitching quality. Equations 6–9 compare the two source patches along the seam after LPAM has explicitly warped one patch toward the other. These metrics therefore inherently favor the intervention while ignoring geometric distortion, duplicated or missing content, and discontinuities at patch boundaries. Evidence for perceptual improvement is inadequate. The main paper provides only one qualitative comparison with complete competing stitchers in Figure 7, without a user study, reference-based synthetic benchmark, artifact measure, per-image results, uncertainty, or significance testing. strengths: The paper targets a genuine practical failure mode in large-parallax stitching. LPAM is a simple, training-free post-alignment module that can be attached to existing seam-cutting pipelines without redesigning their core algorithms.

The evaluation has useful breadth: 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five upstream alignment methods. Tables 1 and 2 report consistent improvements across RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC.

The method is generally easy to follow, with a clear overview, algorithm, parameter ablations, CPU runtime measurements, and appropriate attribution of SSIM, Otsu thresholding, SIFT flow, and graph cuts.
The authors provide a code link and candidly show a failure case where local warping cannot simultaneously achieve alignment and smooth patch boundaries.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evaluation is not sufficiently independent. Equations 6–9 measure agreement between the two locally warped source patches along the resulting seam; LPAM is explicitly designed to make those patches agree, and SSIM also drives patch selection in Equation 2. These scores therefore do not establish perceptual quality of the final mosaic. This concern is illustrated by Table 3: removing the sigmoid often improves the seam metrics even though the paper reports that it introduces visible boundary artifacts.

Direct evidence against competing stitching systems is weak. Figure 7 provides only one main-paper scene comparing LPAM with Parallax and SEAGULL, with no user study, ground-truth evaluation, perceptual assessment, or quantitative final-mosaic comparison. There are also no confidence intervals, significance tests, per-image win rates, or failure frequencies over the 79 pairs.

The originality is modest relative to ICCV standards: the pipeline combines established SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT-flow alignment, and constrained graph-cut seam selection. Its distinction from prior seam-guided local alignment and recent dense-matching seam methods, especially references 22 and 35, is not demonstrated experimentally or analyzed deeply enough to support claims such as a new paradigm or the first arbitrary modular framework.

The failure detector has a substantive blind spot: if seam errors are uniformly high, then max(Q) can still be at most 1.5 times mean(Q), causing a globally poor seam to be declared plausible. SSIM can also react to illumination or content changes rather than geometric misalignment, while the claim that false positives cannot degrade results is neither proven nor empirically tested.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous, including how realignment rectangles and margins are chosen, how overlapping components are ordered or merged, vertical versus horizontal handling of the coordinate-dependent sigmoid, SIFT-flow settings and interpolation, and the precise local seam energy. The new 20-pair dataset also lacks a documented collection protocol, license, and explicit release statement.

The efficiency claim is unclear. In Table 4 the rows labeled +LPAM appear to report LPAM's standalone incremental time rather than total pipeline time; adding 6–10 seconds can approximately double or triple several host seam-cutting runtimes. Image resolutions and other timing details are not reported.

The claimed first modular alignment-compensation framework is insufficiently distinguished from prior seam-guided local alignment such as SEAGULL and recent dense-matching seam methods.

Important technical details are underspecified. Equation 3 also unrealistically assumes exact RGB equality, whereas SIFT Flow matches descriptors under regularization.

weaknesses: The main quantitative evidence is not sufficiently independent. Equations 6–9 measure correspondence between the locally warped inputs around the resulting seam—the exact property LPAM is constructed to improve—and SSIM also drives patch selection. Different methods can additionally be evaluated along different pixels. These scores do not capture geometric distortion, duplicated or missing content, or discontinuities at patch boundaries. Table 3 reinforces this concern: removing the sigmoid produces better metric values while visibly introducing artifacts. A perceptual study, ground-truth evaluation, or independent full-mosaic metric is needed.

The claimed superiority over existing stitching systems is weakly supported. Tables 1 and 2 are primarily before/after comparisons of LPAM, while Figure 7 provides only one direct qualitative example against Microsoft ICE, Parallax, and SEAGULL. There is no quantitative comparison against complete competing systems and no experiment against the recent related methods [5] or [35].

The seam detector has a consequential logical weakness: max(Q) ≤ 1.5 mean(Q) declares a seam plausible even when every pixel has uniformly high error. The assertion that false positives cannot yield inferior results is neither proved nor consistent with the reported artifact cases. Detection accuracy and the choices of k and Otsu threshold are not ablated.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including how alignment-patch margins are chosen, SIFT-flow parameters, SSIM color handling, and the treatment or ordering of overlapping components. The sigmoid taper is defined only using the horizontal coordinate, leaving vertical or irregular seam configurations unclear.

The method is largely a heuristic assembly of SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT flow, sigmoid attenuation, and graph-cut seam estimation. strengths: The paper addresses a practical failure mode in large-parallax stitching with a simple, training-free module that limits expensive dense alignment to problematic seam neighborhoods and can potentially retrofit existing stitching systems.

The evaluation has useful breadth: LPAM is applied to four seam-cutting methods, five initial-alignment methods, and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. Tables 1–2 report consistent improvements across all four metrics and nearly every tested configuration.

The tapered-flow construction and boundary-constrained local seam merging are intuitively motivated ways to reduce discontinuities when reinserting locally aligned patches. Figures 1–3 and 7 communicate the pipeline and several visible corrections clearly.

The authors provide parameter ablations, CPU timings, code, and an explicit failure case. The discussion correctly recognizes the tradeoff between accurate local alignment and consistency with the surrounding image.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is not sufficiently independent of the method. LPAM selects patches using SSIM and explicitly aligns the two source patches, while Eqs. (6)–(9) measure agreement between those locally modified patches along the resulting seam. These scores do not directly measure the perceptual quality, geometric fidelity, or content preservation of the final mosaic. Indeed, Table 3 reports that removing the sigmoid taper gives substantially better metric values even though Figure 3 shows that this setting creates visible artifacts, demonstrating that the chosen metrics can favor an inferior result.

Evidence for final perceptual quality is limited. The manuscript provides only a small number of full-mosaic examples, with essentially one comprehensive cross-method comparison in Figure 7, and no human preference study or suitable independent perceptual evaluation. Results are reported only as dataset means, without dispersion, paired significance tests, or per-image win rates.

The novelty is modest relative to the strength of the claims: LPAM combines established SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT flow, sigmoid weighting, and graph-cut seam estimation. Claims that it “dissociates” seam quality from initial alignment and works with “arbitrary” seam-cutting pipelines are overstated. It still requires the initial seam to traverse locally corresponding content, and the acknowledged failure in Figure 6 shows continued dependence on the initial geometry. The closely related recent dense-matching seam method [35] is discussed but not experimentally compared.

The seam-failure test is technically questionable: max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) measures only relative variation and can classify a uniformly high-error, badly misaligned seam as plausible. The fixed factor 1.5 and Otsu-based selection are not ablated, and the assertion that false-positive local alignments cannot degrade results is unsupported.

Important implementation details are missing from the manuscript, including how enclosing rectangles and margins are chosen, how vertical or oppositely oriented seams are handled, how overlapping extracted components are processed, and the SIFT-flow objective and parameters. Equation (3) assumes exact photometric equality and is not the actual SIFT-flow optimization problem, yet Algorithm 1 states that the flow is obtained from this equation.

The ablation does not convincingly justify the final configuration: beta=16 is often comparable to or better than beta=8, while removing the taper dominates the reported metrics. Runtime is 6–10 seconds per pair on a CPU, but input resolutions and end-to-end latency are not reported. The capture protocol and public availability of the authors’ 20-pair dataset are also unspecified.

LPAM is an intuitive modular pipeline combining seam-quality detection, localized SIFT-Flow alignment, tapered warping, and constrained seam merging. Figures 2–3 and Algorithm 1 communicate the main idea clearly.

The evaluation has useful breadth: four seam-cutting methods, five initial alignment methods, and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. The reported mean seam-quality metrics improve consistently after adding LPAM.

The paper provides parameter studies, CPU timings, a public code URL, and an informative failure case. The discussion candidly identifies the tradeoff between accurate patch alignment and boundary consistency.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative evidence is partly circular. LPAM detects regions using SSIM and warps them to increase local cross-image agreement, while RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC are then measured on patches along the modified, newly selected seam. These scores are not evaluated at common spatial locations and do not independently establish perceptual mosaic quality or geometric correctness.

This metric limitation is visible in Table 3: removing the sigmoid taper produces substantially better numerical scores, yet the authors report that it creates visible boundary artifacts. Thus, the metrics used for the main claims demonstrably miss an important class of failure.

There is no aggregate quantitative or human-preference comparison against complete state-of-the-art stitching systems. Parallax, SEAGULL, and Microsoft ICE are compared principally through the single example in Figure 7; no uncertainty, significance tests, per-image distributions, or failure rates are reported.

Originality is modest: SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT Flow, graph-cut seam estimation, and tapered local warping are established components. The distinction from prior seam-driven and dense-flow seam-estimation approaches—especially reference [35]—is not sufficiently developed experimentally. Claims of a new paradigm that “dissociates” quality from initial alignment are overstated because LPAM still depends on the initial warp and local correspondence quality.

Important implementation details are missing, including how enclosing patches are expanded, how taper direction is chosen for arbitrary seam orientations, SIFT-Flow and graph-cut parameters, local energy terms, and handling of overlapping patches, borders, occlusions, or update order. Equation 5 also only approaches, rather than attains, the stated endpoint constraints. These omissions weaken reproducibility and the claim of compatibility with arbitrary pipelines.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical failure mode in large-parallax stitching and proposes an appealing modular repair stage that can augment existing alignment and seam-cutting pipelines.

The method is intuitive and reasonably coherent: seam-local SSIM identifies problematic regions, SIFT Flow performs localized realignment, and tapered warping plus boundary-constrained seam merging aims to avoid patch-boundary artifacts. Figures 2 and 3 explain the pipeline effectively.

The evaluation has useful breadth: 79 image pairs from three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods. Tables 1 and 2 report consistent improvements across RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC.
The paper includes parameter ablations, runtime measurements, a concrete failure case, an appropriate limitations discussion, and a public code link.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest because LPAM primarily combines established components—SSIM/Otsu thresholding, SIFT Flow, sigmoid tapering, and graph-cut seam optimization. Claims such as “first modular framework,” “arbitrary seam-cutting pipelines,” and dissociation from initial alignment accuracy are stronger than the evidence, particularly given closely related seam-guided local-alignment work such as SEAGULL and dense-matching method [35].

The principal quantitative evaluation is partly circular: SSIM-like patch disagreement selects the regions to repair, and RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and ZNCC between the same locally warped image patches then measure success. These metrics do not directly assess final-mosaic artifacts or geometric/content distortion. Indeed, Table 3 shows that removing the sigmoid yields the best metric values despite introducing visible artifacts, demonstrating this mismatch.

Evidence for perceptual superiority is limited. The main paper provides only one full comparison example in Figure 7, no user study or robust perceptual evaluation, and no quantitative final-output comparison against Parallax, SEAGULL, or the recent dense-matching approach [35]. Means are reported without per-image distributions, uncertainty, or significance tests.

The seam-failure detector can miss uniformly poor seams: when all seam pixels have similarly high error, max(Q) can remain below 1.5 times mean(Q), causing the seam to be declared plausible. There is no ablation of this threshold, detection accuracy analysis, or characterization of how often LPAM activates and fails.

Several details needed to assess soundness and reproduce the method are underspecified, including extracted-patch margins, handling of curved/vertical seams and overlapping components, processing order, the exact local seam energy, and SIFT Flow settings. Equation 3 assumes unattainable exact photometric correspondence, while the horizontal sigmoid construction is not fully generalized or justified.

The custom 20-pair dataset lacks acquisition, resolution, licensing, and release details. Table 4 is also ambiguous about whether “+LPAM” denotes overhead or total integrated runtime, excludes initial alignment, and omits image-resolution and precise CPU information. Overall, the idea has practical merit, but novelty and perceptually relevant validation remain insufficient for acceptance at the ICCV bar.

The evaluation has useful breadth: 79 image pairs across three datasets, four seam-cutting methods, and five initial alignment methods. LPAM consistently improves all reported seam-agreement metrics in Tables 1 and 2.

The authors provide parameter ablations, CPU timings, a failure example, and a public-code link. The pipeline and figures are generally easy to follow, and reused methods and public datasets are mostly attributed.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evidence is not an independent measure of panorama quality. LPAM detects regions using SSIM, warps those same image patches to increase local correspondence, reselects the seam, and is then evaluated using SSIM and closely correlated patch-agreement metrics along that modified seam. These measurements can improve without producing a more geometrically natural or perceptually preferable mosaic. There is no ground truth, human study, independent perceptual assessment, or per-example/statistical analysis, while the main paper provides only one full qualitative comparison scene.

The failure detector is logically unreliable: the rule max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) accepts a uniformly poor seam whenever all its errors are similarly high because it contains no absolute-quality criterion. SSIM can also confuse exposure or content changes with misalignment and miss shifts in low-texture regions. The unsupported assertion that false-positive realignment cannot worsen results is especially problematic under occlusion, repeated texture, or moving objects.

The technical formulation does not justify several core claims. Equation (3) assumes exact RGB equality after displacement and is neither the SIFT-flow objective nor generally satisfiable in occluded or photometrically different regions. The sigmoid has nonzero displacement at one boundary and nearly full displacement at the other, while an x-only taper cannot guarantee continuity along all four patch boundaries. Consequently, the claimed smooth consistency is not established, and applicability appears restricted to horizontally arranged two-image overlaps.

The ablation weakens the design choice: removing the sigmoid produces better values than beta=8 in 10 of the 12 reported metric cells. The authors justify retaining it with one artifact illustration but supply no quantitative boundary-artifact or perceptual evaluation. There are also no ablations for the 1.5 threshold, Otsu segmentation, selective patch detection, flow confidence, or constrained local seam.

The novelty and scope are overstated. The method combines established SSIM, SIFT flow, and graph-cut components, and seam-guided local alignment is already closely represented by SEAGULL. Experiments support compatibility with several hard-label pairwise seam methods, not the claimed arbitrary seam-cutting pipelines or a genuine dissociation from initial alignment quality.

Important implementation details are missing, including how component rectangles are expanded, how overlapping patches are ordered or reconciled, SIFT-flow and graph-cut parameters, treatment of vertical seams and out-of-bounds warps, and image resolutions. The 20-pair in-house dataset lacks provenance and release information. Timing rows report LPAM separately rather than complete end-to-end runtime and omit variability, limiting reproducibility and the efficiency claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear practical failure mode in large-parallax stitching: seam cutting cannot conceal severe local misalignment. The proposed seam-triggered local refinement is intuitive and potentially useful as a plug-in.

LPAM combines seam-quality detection, localized SIFT-flow alignment, tapered warping, and boundary-constrained local seam cutting into a coherent pipeline. The seam-merging constraint is a sensible design choice for avoiding junction artifacts.

Evaluation spans three datasets comprising 79 image pairs, four seam-cutting methods, and five initial alignment methods. The consistently improved aggregate seam-agreement scores suggest that the module is not tied to one particular upstream pipeline.

The paper includes parameter ablations, CPU timing, qualitative comparisons, explicit failure cases, and a code link. The presentation and figures are generally clear, and relevant constituent methods are appropriately cited.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not sufficiently independent of the method. LPAM detects patches using SSIM and explicitly warps them to increase local correspondence, while all four quantitative metrics are again computed between source patches along the resulting seam. These scores do not measure distortions, discontinuities around repaired patches, duplicated content, or overall perceptual mosaic quality. Indeed, Table 3 reports that removing the sigmoid gives substantially better metrics while Figure 3 shows worse artifacts, directly demonstrating this metric-objective mismatch. A user study, reference-based evaluation, or systematic perceptual/artifact assessment is needed.

Evidence for superiority over complete state-of-the-art stitching systems is limited to a single main-paper qualitative example. Tables 1 and 2 are primarily before/after tests of the proposed module, not quantitative comparisons of final mosaics against Parallax, SEAGULL, or the closely related 2025 dense-matching seam method [35]. No uncertainty, per-image distributions, or significance tests are reported.

The novelty is modest and the claims are overstated. SSIM/Otsu selection, SIFT flow, sigmoid tapering, and graph-cut seam cutting are established components. LPAM does not truly “dissociate” seam quality from initial alignment: it requires a usable overlap and initial seam, assumes failures are localized, and its own failure analysis shows dependence on the extracted patch and initial geometry.

The failure detector is technically fragile: max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) labels a seam plausible based on relative variation, so a uniformly severe misalignment can be accepted without repair. The assertion that false-positive patch alignment cannot degrade results is unsupported and conflicts with the reported artifact examples. There is no ablation or detection analysis for k, Otsu thresholding, or localization accuracy.

Important implementation details are missing, including how component-enclosing patch margins are chosen, how horizontal versus vertical or curved seam segments determine the taper direction, SIFT-flow settings and occlusion handling, behavior for overlapping patches and processing order, and the precise local seam energy. Equation (3)'s exact photometric equality is also unrealistic. These omissions weaken technical clarity despite the available code link.

Experimental reporting contains reproducibility concerns: the new 20-pair dataset lacks a capture protocol, resolutions, licensing, and an explicit availability statement; the SEAGULL entries for Perception and Iterative in Table 1 are exactly duplicated across all metrics before and after LPAM; and Table 4 ambiguously presents “+LPAM” time separately rather than clearly reporting end-to-end totals, obscuring that overhead can approximately double simpler pipelines.
